title: Entropy contraction on complete bipartite graphs via reverse erasure: only the rarest symbol matters
shortTitle: Only the rarest symbol matters: entropy contraction for reverse erasure and complete bipartite graphs
oneLine: The worst-case entropy loss of reverse erasure depends only on the rarest symbol, which settles a complete-bipartite conjecture.
abstract: Caputo, Chen, Gu and Polyanskiy (2025) conjectured that one step of the half-lazy random walk on the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} keeps at most the fraction log n / (2 log 2n) of relative entropy, with single vertices as the only worst starts, and proved the case n = 3 with computer assistance. This candidate proves the conjecture for every n, and for K_{m,n} with M = max(m, n). One step of the walk splits into two copies of the reverse-erasure channel: keep the current symbol with probability α, otherwise redraw it from a prior ρ. For this channel the relative-entropy contraction coefficient depends on the prior only through its smallest atom q, at every α. Up to the sharp threshold α = q^{q/(1−q)} it equals log(1/q)/log(1/(αq)), attained only at a rarest point input; the upper bound is a translation of a weighted mean inequality of Gao, and the uniform binary case is known (Nair and Wang; Zhao). Above the threshold the worst inputs are full-support exponential tilts and no closed form is given. Further results: a rank-one weighted extension that settles the lazy-star observation of Jadhav (2026); a reduction of any block-reset chain (any laziness, all powers, stars, multipartite graphs) to a chain with at most two states per block, whose values are then computed numerically; and the exact one-way agreement-distillation rate below the threshold. There is no mixing-time improvement: the spectral gap is 1/2. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

evidence: Written informal proofs of every theorem, proposition and corollary in a 27-page manuscript. Four verification scripts with recorded outputs in normal and optimised Python: a random-sample suite (101 gates, including 88,736 full-matrix bipartite inputs), minimum-mass reduction diagnostics, ten must-fail negative controls (all detected) with structured near-extremiser families, and 122 numerical checks of the block-reset extension with five must-fail controls; exact rational fingerprints of small kernels. All were rerun from a fresh copy with and without Python -O and matched the recorded results exactly, apart from timing and version fields.

keyResults: Only the rarest symbol matters (Theorem 2.3, proof): the relative-entropy contraction coefficient of the reverse-erasure channel depends on the prior only through its smallest atom q, at every retention probability α, with an exact one-variable test (Proposition 2.4).

Closed form and sharp threshold (Theorem 2.5, proof): for α ≤ q^{q/(1−q)} the coefficient is log(1/q)/log(1/(αq)), attained only at a rarest point input; the threshold is sharp. The upper bound translates Gao's weighted mean inequality.
Above the threshold (Proposition 2.6, Theorem 2.7, proof): the local coefficient is α and the worst inputs are full-support exponential tilts; no closed form is given.

The conjecture (Theorem 6.1, Corollary 6.2, proof): the half-lazy walk on K_{m,n} keeps at most log M/(2 log 2M) of relative entropy, M = max(m, n), with only point extremisers for M ≥ 3; also rank-one weights and the lazy star K_{1,N}.

Block-reset chains (Section 7, proof of the reduction): any laziness, all powers, stars and multipartite graphs reduce to a chain with at most two states per block; the values there are computed numerically.
Agreement distillation (Corollary 8.1, proof): below the threshold the exact one-way rate is log(1/α)/log(1/(αq)) when the party holding the erased copy speaks.

narration: Only the rarest symbol matters. An Evidence Press briefing. Imagine a noisy channel that sometimes erases what you send. Now run it backwards: you keep each symbol with some probability, and otherwise replace it with a fresh random draw from a fixed prior. A natural question is how much of the surprise of an input, measured by relative entropy, can survive one such step in the worst case. You might expect the answer to depend on the whole prior. It does not. This paper proves that it depends only on the probability of the rarest symbol. Two priors that share the same smallest probability, such as one tenth, two tenths and seven tenths, or one tenth and nine tenths, give exactly the same answer. Up to a sharp threshold there is an exact formula; above it, the worst inputs change shape and no closed formula is given. The key inequality is a known result of Gao, which the paper credits. The application is a lazy random walk on a complete bipartite graph: stay put half the time, otherwise jump to a random vertex on the other side. In 2025, Caputo, Chen, Gu and Polyanskiy conjectured the exact worst-case entropy loss of this walk and checked it by computer for three vertices per side. The paper proves it for every size, and extends the method to any laziness, matrix powers, stars and multipartite graphs, where the problem shrinks to a chain with a few states that is then solved numerically. It does not speed up mixing times. The proofs are written out, with numerical checks and negative controls. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed. Published on the third of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Whether a worst-case entropy retention bound for a reverse-erasure step or a rank-one block-reset chain can be computed from the smallest prior probability alone (yes, by an exact formula below the threshold and a one-variable test above it) instead of an optimisation over all inputs.
decisionObject.scope: One-step fixed-reference KL contraction of the reverse-erasure channel and of rank-one block-reset chains. No closed form above the threshold; values for other laziness, powers and multipartite graphs are numerical; no mixing-time claim.
